topic: Deciding whether a relation is a function
subtitle: One input, one output: tables, lists of pairs, graphs, and rules

problems.desc: Part (b): decision, with reasoning, about whether the table defines a function. Full credit requires the student to say that it does, because every input in the top row appears once and so is paired with exactly one output. Accept an answer that says no input is repeated. Do not accept 'yes' with no reference to inputs having a single output.

problems.slot: (b) the two outputs of the repeated input

problems.desc: Part (c): decision, with reasoning, about whether the list of pairs is a function. Full credit requires the student to say that it is not, because the input 5 appears in two pairs with two different outputs, and a function allows each input only one output. Accept an answer that names the offending input and both of its outputs. Do not accept 'no' on its own.

Part (b): decision, with reasoning, about whether graph P shows a function. Full credit requires the student to say that it does, because no two plotted points sit directly above each other, so no input value has more than one output. Accept the vertical-line-test wording: any vertical line meets the plotted points at most once. Do not accept 'yes' with no test named.

problems.slot: (b) the two outputs of the repeated input

problems.desc: Part (c): decision, with reasoning, about whether the table defines a function. Full credit requires the student to say that it does not, because the input 8 appears in two columns paired with two different outputs, 12 and 8, and a function allows only one output per input. Accept an answer that names the repeated input and both outputs. Do not accept a bare no.

Part (b): decision, with reasoning, about whether graph Q shows a function. Full credit requires the student to say that it does not, because two plotted points sit directly above each other, so one input value is paired with two different outputs. Accept the vertical-line-test wording: a vertical line drawn through those points meets the graph twice. Do not accept a bare no.

Part (b): decision, with reasoning, about whether the list of pairs is a function even though the output repeats. Full credit requires the student to say that it is a function: the rule restricts inputs, not outputs, and here every input appears once and has exactly one output, so several inputs sharing the output 4 is allowed. Do not accept 'no, because the outputs repeat', which is the misconception this problem targets.

problems.slot: (b) the two outputs of the repeated input in S

problems.desc: Part (c): decision, with reasoning, about which of the two relations is a function. Full credit requires the student to say that R is a function because each of its inputs appears once, while S is not because the input 4 appears twice with the different outputs 3 and 11. Accept an answer that checks each relation in turn against the one-output-per-input rule. Do not accept a choice with no reason.

Part (b): explanation of why a rule always defines a function while a list of pairs need not. Full credit requires the student to say that a rule performs the same arithmetic on any input and can therefore return only one result for it, whereas a list is written by hand and can happen to contain the same input twice with different outputs. Accept an answer that tests the rule on one input and notes that the calculation has only one possible outcome. Do not accept a restatement of the definition with no comparison of the two forms.
